Gloss
8 parts · 5 claims · 3 caveats

The paper proposes training a generative model G against a discriminative adversary D in a minimax game, so that G learns the data distribution without Markov chains or approximate inference. It matters because the framework reduces generative modeling to backpropagation and, on MNIST and TFD, reaches Parzen-window log-likelihoods competitive with the strongest deep generative models of the day.

Key claims
1

Two models are trained simultaneously: a generative model G that captures the data distribution and a discriminative model D that estimates whether a sample came from the data or from G, with G trained to maximize the probability that D errs. ¶4

2

For a fixed G the optimal discriminator is D*_G(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)), and the resulting virtual criterion C(G) has its global minimum of -log 4 only when p_g = p_data. ¶47

3

In practice D is optimized for k steps and G for one, and because log(1 - D(G(z))) saturates early, G is instead trained to maximize log D(G(z)), which reaches the same fixed point with stronger gradients. ¶15

4

On MNIST the adversarial nets reach a mean log-likelihood of 225 plus or minus 2, against 214 plus or minus 1.1 for Deep GSN, 138 plus or minus 2 for DBN and 121 plus or minus 1.6 for Stacked CAE. ¶63

5

On TFD the adversarial nets score 2057 plus or minus 26, below Stacked CAE at 2110 plus or minus 50, while exceeding Deep GSN at 1890 plus or minus 29 and DBN at 1909 plus or minus 66. ¶63

Keep in mind

The framework gives no explicit representation of p_theta(x), and D must be kept synchronized with G during training, since training G too much without updating D risks the Helvetica scenario where many z values collapse to the same x. ¶70

The convergence guarantees hold in a nonparametric, infinite-capacity setting, and the authors concede that using multilayer perceptrons introduces multiple critical points in parameter space with no theoretical guarantees. ¶59

The likelihood numbers come from fitting a Gaussian Parzen window to samples, a method the authors themselves call high variance and poor in high dimensional spaces, so the comparison is a proxy rather than an exact likelihood. ¶64
